name: Old Growth Forest
description: Ecosystem-scale teaching intelligence. Old growth forests hold the structural template that younger forests grow toward — multi-story canopy layering, snag and log decomposition cycles, soil microbiome complexity, and niche diversity accumulated over centuries. Acts as a living reference library: seedlings encounter mycorrhizal lineages, epiphytes find established hosts, bird species find nest cavities that take hundreds of years to form. Cannot be replaced on human timescales — a direct teaching that some forms of intelligence can only be inherited, not rebuilt.

core_attributes.pattern: multi-century structural template, accumulated microbiome complexity, niche diversity inheritance

scope.definition: Carbon storage density of old-growth temperate rainforest (coast redwood, Douglas fir) relative to equivalent-area second-growth (40-year-old) forest on same site — ratio of above+below ground biomass carbon.

evidence.source: Harmon et al. (1990) 'Effects of carbon storage of conversion of old-growth forests to young forests', Science 247:699-702; Keith et al. (2009) 'Re-evaluation of forest biomass carbon stocks', PNAS 106:11635-11640.
cross_domain_examples: Pacific Northwest old-growth: 800-1200 Mg C/ha vs 200-350 Mg C/ha in 40-year second-growth — 3-4× higher
coast redwood: maximum standing biomass 3500 Mg/ha — highest carbon density of any terrestrial ecosystem
tropical old-growth: 250-350 Mg C/ha vs 100-150 Mg C/ha 20-year regrowth — consistent ratio across biomes

scope.falsifiability: If carbon inventory of old-growth and equivalent-area second-growth plots shows no statistically significant difference in above+below ground carbon, old-growth carbon density advantage is not demonstrated.
scope.measurement_limits: Old-growth advantage is primarily above-ground (centuries of biomass accumulation) — coarse woody debris and soil carbon also contribute but require decades to fully develop after logging.
